analysis.one_liner: Limits secret court orders for phone and email surveillance and requires targets be told and orders unsealed.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support in February 2026 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for how law enforcement surveils people's phones, email, and online records. Courts could only keep a surveillance order sealed for 180 days at a time, with progressively harder showings to keep extending the seal, and orders would be automatically unsealed and published once a seal expires. People whose communications or records are collected would have to be notified, unless a court finds — on a certified, reviewable basis — that notice would endanger someone, cause flight, destroy evidence, or intimidate witnesses. It would also require annual public reports on how often these orders are sought and granted, and tie federal recognition of state and tribal warrants to courts adopting the same transparency rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose phones, email, or online records are searched by federal, state, or tribal law enforcement. Today, targets of these orders often never find out, and the orders themselves can stay sealed indefinitely. The bill guarantees eventual notice to the target and public unsealing, and it lets any member of the public go to court to unseal a surveillance order. Journalists and researchers would also gain from public dockets and annual reports showing which agencies are requesting which kinds of surveillance.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees that a person whose communications or records are collected by law enforcement will eventually receive notice of the surveillance, with any delay capped at 180-day periods and subject to judicial review.

Prohibits indefinite sealing: a surveillance order, application, or inventory can only be sealed for 180 days at a time, extensions after the first require a 'particularized showing' including the target's name and specific facts, and courts must automatically unseal orders the business day after a seal expires.

Lets any person — not just the surveilled target — ask a court to unseal a surveillance order or challenge redactions, with the government paying that person's legal fees if they substantially prevail.

Requires public, machine-readable dockets for surveillance cases and annual public reports on every application for surveillance and gag orders, so the scale of secret surveillance becomes countable for the first time.
Closes a known gap by requiring courts to order an inventory whenever a provider hands over data beyond what a court authorized, and to tell the target about it.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies would lose indefinite secrecy and indefinite delayed notice — the tools they currently use to keep surveillance and its targets hidden. Federal, state, and tribal courts would take on new docketing, publication, and annual reporting work, funded by up to $26 million in authorized appropriations and grants. Investigators argue that early unsealing can tip off targets and compromise cases; the bill accepts that risk in exchange for transparency.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and court systems

drawbacks.text: Sealed records and delayed notice exist to protect investigations — to keep targets from fleeing, destroying evidence, or intimidating witnesses. The bill keeps that tool but time-limits it; if its 180-day windows and escalating showings prove too tight, ongoing investigations could be compromised.

Publishing surveillance orders and dockets could expose sensitive personal information about the people surveilled, including people never charged with anything; the bill directs the Supreme Court to write rules protecting personal information in the published records, but the risk is acknowledged in the bill itself.

Many state and tribal courts lack electronic docketing systems; the bill gives them up to four years to comply and authorizes $25 million in grants, but implementation would still be a real lift for smaller court systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design shows real care about the strongest objection: it preserves secrecy during active investigations but time-limits it, makes each extension harder to get, and routes disputes to a judge. The main cost is operational — paperwork and systems for courts, and some risk to ongoing investigations when seals lapse — weighed against giving people the basic right to know their government read their communications. As written, the transparency benefits substantially outweigh the costs, though the bill's fate will depend on whether the details survive committee scrutiny.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up, so it sits waiting for the committee to act before the Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the Government Surveillance Transparency Act of 2026 on February 25, 2026, joined by Senators Mike Lee and Steve Daines (Republicans) and Cory Booker (Democrat).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, where it has received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
Its three cosponsors split evenly across parties: two Republicans and one Democrat, in addition to the Democratic sponsor.

The core of the bill is a new chapter in title 18 that caps sealing of surveillance orders at renewable 180-day periods with heightened judicial review for extensions, requires automatic unsealing, and mandates that surveilled persons receive notice unless a court approves a certified delay.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, no one has gained or lost: law enforcement's current practices of indefinite sealing and delayed notice continue, and surveilled people still have no guaranteed notice. If the bill dies in committee, the parties better off will be those who benefit from the surveillance status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement keeps current secrecy practices

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled in the 119th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred on February 25, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Support so far is small but genuinely bipartisan — two Democrats and two Republicans — and no senator has publicly opposed the bill; opposition or indifference has taken the form of committee inaction rather than votes.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and tribal)
industries.note: Agencies would lose the ability to keep surveillance orders sealed indefinitely and to delay telling targets indefinitely. Their operational interest in secrecy in this bill runs directly against the public's interest in knowing when their communications are searched.

industries.industry: Electronic communication and cloud service providers
industries.note: Providers currently operate under non-disclosure (gag) orders of indefinite duration; the bill time-limits those orders to the life of a 180-day renewable seal and requires the government to tell them and the court when it seeks data beyond a court's authorization. Clearer, bounded rules align with the public's transparency interest.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and tribal court systems
industries.note: Courts take on new publication, docketing, and annual reporting duties, funded by a $1 million appropriation and a $25 million grant program for state and tribal courts, with phase-in periods for courts that lack electronic systems. The burden is real but paid for and phased.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with four total sponsors and no scheduled action, and the session ends January 3, 2027. Unless the committee schedules a hearing or markup in the coming months, this bill will die at the end of the Congress without a vote, as most bills do; its bipartisan sponsorship is a starting point, but at this stage it has no movement.
